mstts:express-as.prosody: Early Struggles and the Search for Safety. You know, there comes a point in a lot of our lives when the world just feels too loud. Maybe you've felt it—the urge to find some quiet, even if it's just for a moment. For many people, that search for peace starts early, whether it's in the stillness of a childhood bedroom or right in the middle of a noisy school hallway. It's not always happiness we're after. Sometimes, it's just about feeling safe—finding a spot where your heart can finally take a breath. Picture a young girl growing up in what seems like a regular family. She's got parents who care, siblings who bicker, and a home that looks perfectly fine from the outside. But inside, she feels this constant ache—like something about her isn’t quite right. The world seems to want her to be a shinier, quieter, easier-to-love version of herself. She picks up pretty quickly that certain feelings—like anger, or sadness, even real joy—are better kept hidden. So, she tucks them away, hoping that being "good enough" will finally make the discomfort fade. School turns into a stage. She watches other kids, studying their every move, trying to crack the code—What do they wear? How do they talk? She copies their laughter, their interests, even their silences. But the more she tries to blend in, the more out of place she feels. The pressure keeps building, and with it, a kind of loneliness that's tough to put into words. Then adolescence hits, and that ache? It only gets sharper. The world’s expectations feel heavier than ever, and the gap between who she really is and who everyone wants her to be just seems to grow. Food becomes both a comfort and a weapon. She learns how to control her hunger, how to shrink herself—almost hoping she can disappear. The little rituals of restriction and secrecy give her a strange sense of relief. It’s power, in a world that can feel so overwhelming. But that relief never lasts. The emptiness always comes back, even stronger. So, she searches for new ways to escape—maybe alcohol, maybe parties, anything that gives her a break from the constant self-critique. Sure, each distraction brings its own set of problems, but for a while, they help keep the pain away. Of course, family members start to notice changes. Some try to help, some look the other way. She gets really good at hiding her struggles, always showing the world a polished version of herself. She becomes an expert at pretending, even as she feels herself slipping further away from who she once was. And in those quiet moments, she wonders—does anyone else feel like this? She’s pretty sure they do, but nobody talks about it. That silence? It becomes another weight she carries, following her into adulthood. The search for safety keeps going, but the path isn’t clear. What she doesn’t know yet is that real healing won’t come from running away. It’ll take turning toward her pain, facing it head-on, and finally giving herself the chance to breathe.
